paragraphs.heading: Lava and lava flows
paragraphs.text: Lava is magma that has been expelled onto the surface of a terrestrial planet, such as Earth, or of a moon, from its interior. It can erupt at a volcano or through a crack in the crust, on land or underwater, and its temperature is usually between 800 and 1,200 °C. When lava pours out during an effusive eruption, the outpouring is called a lava flow. An explosive eruption is different: what comes out is tephra, a mix of volcanic ash with other fragments, and not lava flows.

paragraphs.heading: Thick, yet far-travelling
paragraphs.text: Most molten lava is about as viscous as ketchup, which is roughly 10,000 to 100,000 times as viscous as water. Even so, lava can travel great distances before cooling makes it solid. Lava exposed to air quickly grows a solid crust. The crust insulates the liquid lava that remains, which helps keep it hot and runny enough to go on flowing.

paragraphs.heading: Silica sets the thickness
paragraphs.text: The silica in a silicate magma dominates how it behaves physically. Lava that is high in silica is much more viscous than lava that is low in silica. Temperature and many other properties of a lava are also seen to go along with its silica content. For these reasons silicate lavas are split into four chemical types by how much silica they hold: felsic, intermediate, mafic and ultramafic.

paragraphs.heading: Felsic lava
paragraphs.text: Felsic lavas are more than 63% silica, and they include rhyolite and dacite lavas. With so much silica they are extremely viscous. Because of that very high viscosity, felsic lavas usually erupt explosively and leave deposits of fragments. Now and then a rhyolite lava does erupt effusively, forming lava spines, lava domes or thick, short lava flows called coulees. Unusually hot rhyolite lavas, above 950 °C, may flow for many tens of kilometres.

paragraphs.heading: Intermediate lava
paragraphs.text: Intermediate lavas, also called andesitic lavas, contain 52% to 63% silica. They are commonly hotter than felsic lavas, at 850 to 1,100 °C. Lower silica and higher eruptive temperatures make them much less viscous as a rule. Their typical viscosity is a little greater than that of smooth peanut butter.

paragraphs.heading: Mafic lava
paragraphs.text: Mafic lavas, also called basaltic lavas, are marked by relatively high magnesium oxide and iron oxide content, and their silica content stays between 45% and 52%. They generally erupt at 1,100 to 1,200 °C and at relatively low viscosities. Their viscosity is similar to that of ketchup, though still many orders of magnitude higher than water's. Because this less viscous lava can flow a long way from the vent, mafic lavas tend to build low-profile shield volcanoes or flood basalts.

paragraphs.heading: A flow that inflates
paragraphs.text: A basaltic lava flow that has gone solid can be much thicker than the moving molten flow ever was at any one moment, particularly on a low slope. Basaltic lavas may "inflate". More lava keeps arriving, and it presses on the crust that has already hardened. Underwater, basaltic lavas can form pillow lavas.
